645.title: Kumbhakarna and tamas
645.hook: Ravana loses his first duel, and orders the giant who sleeps for months to be woken
645.carry: kumbhakarna is tamas: the sleep that misses what matters
645.howItsDone: The waking of Kumbhakarna is a favorite scene in Ramlila and in shadow-puppet traditions, often played for laughs; in many Indian families a heavy sleeper is teasingly called Kumbhakarna.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Garuda's old story. Two sisters, a cheat, a son who freed his mother, and the bird who carries Vishnu. vahana: garuda's strength bows to vishnu.

Ravana finally rides out himself. He strikes Lakshmana down with a great spear and tries to lift him to carry him off, and can't move him. Hanuman can, easily, and carries Lakshmana to safety. Then Rama meets Ravana, smashes his chariot, and cuts the crown from his head. And Rama stops. You've fought hard today, he says, and you're tired. Go home and rest. Come back tomorrow, and see what I can do. Ravana goes home alive, beaten, humiliated. And he gives an order: wake my brother.
screen: `RAVANA RIDES OUT.` → `GO HOME AND REST.` → `WAKE MY BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Ravana's brother is Kumbhakarna, and his name says it: pot-ears. He's a giant beyond giants, and he sleeps. Not for a night. For months. Waking him is a comic set piece in the war book. Rakshasas pile up mountains of food beside him. They beat drums and blow conches by his ears, hit him with clubs, and march elephants over his body. Nothing. Finally he yawns, stretches, and wakes up hungry. Why does he sleep like that? Valmiki gives two answers. In one, Brahma, the creator, cursed the greedy young giant to sleep as if dead, then softened it at Ravana's pleading: six months asleep, one day awake. In the other, as Kumbhakarna was about to ask Brahma for a boon, the goddess Sarasvati entered his speech, and the boon he asked for was sleep. Hindu teachers have long seen more than a joke here. The Bhagavad Gita names three gunas, three strands woven through everything, our minds included: sattva, clarity; rajas, restless wanting; and tamas, heaviness. Tamas, it says, binds us through carelessness, laziness and sleep. Many teachers read Lanka's three brothers as those three strands: Ravana, all wanting; Vibhishana, clear; and Kumbhakarna, tamas, asleep while his own city fights for its life. In many Indian homes, a teenager who sleeps till noon gets called Kumbhakarna. It's a tease, and a teaching: the heaviness in us can sleep straight through what matters, until something shakes it awake.
screen: `KUMBHAKARNA: POT-EARS.` · `DRUMS, CLUBS AND ELEPHANTS.` · `A CURSE, OR A TWISTED BOON.` · `SATTVA, RAJAS, TAMAS.` · then, large: `TAMAS: THE SLEEP THAT MISSES WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Sit up tall, the opposite of a sleeper, and let light into your eyes. Take three deep breaths that wake the body. If you pray, you might whisper the close of the Gayatri, the morning prayer many Hindus say: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, may that light stir our minds. If you don't, name one thing you've been sleeping through, and set it in front of you for today.
Kumbhakarna. Ravana's giant brother, pot-ears, who sleeps for months, and whom many teachers read as tamas, the heaviness that sleeps through what matters.
Your line: kumbhakarna is tamas, the sleep that misses what matters. Awake now, the giant has something to tell his brother. Day six hundred forty-five.

646.title: Two brothers, two choices
646.hook: the giant tells his brother he's wrong, and goes to fight for him anyway
646.carry: dharma first, even before a brother
646.howItsDone: Kumbhakarna's rebuke of Ravana and his loyalty are much discussed in Ramayana storytelling, and Kamban's Tamil scene of the two brothers, Vibhishana and Kumbhakarna, meeting on the battlefield is often recited.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kumbhakarna, the giant who sleeps for months, woken with drums and elephants because Ravana was losing. kumbhakarna is tamas: the sleep that misses what matters.

Kumbhakarna walks into Ravana's hall, still huge with sleep, and Ravana pours it all out. Rama has crossed the sea. Our best warriors are dead. I lost today. You're the only one left who can save us. The court waits for the giant's roar. And Kumbhakarna, the brother known for sleeping and eating, says what only Vibhishana has said to the king's face, and Vibhishana was driven out for it.
screen: `RAVANA POURS IT OUT.` → `YOU'RE THE ONLY ONE LEFT.` → `THE GIANT SPEAKS PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: We told you, he says. At your council, this is exactly what we said would happen. A king who acts first and thinks afterward, who ignores good advice, brings disaster on himself. You took another man's wife. This is the result. Ravana's face darkens. He wants a champion, not a lecture. And Kumbhakarna sees his brother hurting, and softens. Enough, he says. Whatever you did, I'm your brother. I'll go and kill your enemy. On the battlefield he's terrifying. The monkeys scatter, and Angada has to shame them into turning back. He seizes Sugriva and carries him off under his arm, until Sugriva tears at the giant's ears and nose and escapes. In the end Rama brings him down with his arrows. The Tamil poet Kamban adds a scene. Before the fight, Vibhishana comes to his brother on the field and begs him to join Rama. Kumbhakarna refuses gently: you did right, you stay with Rama; my place is with our brother. So the Ramayana sets two brothers side by side, and both told Ravana the truth to his face. One left to stand with dharma, what is right, and Rama welcomed him. The other let love for his brother carry him into a wrong war, and fell. Many readers admire Kumbhakarna's honesty and his loyalty. But the epic honors Vibhishana's choice. Telling the truth isn't enough if you then march with the wrong. Dharma first, even before a brother.

segments.voice: Think of someone you love who is doing something you know isn't right. If you pray, hold them before God by name, and ask for what Vibhishana had: the courage to be honest and kind at once. If you don't, breathe in their name, and breathe out the true thing you'd say to them, gently.
Kumbhakarna. The giant who tells Ravana plainly he's wrong, and then dies fighting for him out of a brother's loyalty, beside Vibhishana, who chose dharma.
Your line: dharma first, even before a brother. Lakshmana's best day, and his worst, is next. See you then.

647.title: Rama, who keeps the bounds
647.hook: Lakshmana's greatest victory, and the same day, Indrajit comes back with Brahma's weapon
647.carry: maryada: lines rama won't cross, even to win
647.howItsDone: Rama is widely called Maryada Purushottama, the best of men who keeps the bounds, and tellers often point to his choice to endure Brahma's weapon, set beside the serpent-arrows earlier in the war.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kumbhakarna told Ravana plainly he was wrong, then fought for him anyway, and fell. dharma first, even before a brother.

With Kumbhakarna gone, Ravana sends out his other sons. One of them, Atikaya, is a giant in armor that Brahma himself gave him, and no arrow will go through it. Lakshmana fights him a long time, getting nowhere. Then, Valmiki says, the wind god Vayu comes close and whispers in Lakshmana's ear: that armor came from Brahma. Only Brahma's own weapon will break it. Lakshmana takes the hint, and Atikaya falls. It's Lakshmana's great victory. It doesn't last the day.
screen: `ATIKAYA IN BRAHMA'S ARMOR.` → `THE WIND WHISPERS.` → `LAKSHMANA'S GREAT VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Indrajit comes back. Several of his brothers, his uncle Kumbhakarna and a string of champions are dead, and he's furious. This time he prepares. Before he rides out, he makes offerings into a sacred fire, and he comes out with a chariot that can't be seen. Then, from out of sight again, he invokes the weapon of Brahma, the creator. It isn't one arrow. It's a storm. Valmiki pictures the whole field covered: Sugriva, Angada, Jambavan, Nila, leader after leader falling. And Rama does something surprising. He knows what this weapon is, and he chooses not to fight it. This is Brahma's weapon, he tells Lakshmana; it deserves respect. Let's endure it. So the two brothers stand in the rain of arrows and fall, side by side once again. Indrajit rides home in triumph. Hanuman did the same thing in Lanka, when Indrajit bound him with this very weapon: he honored Brahma's power and let himself be bound. This is why Hindus call Rama Maryada Purushottama, the best of men, who keeps the maryada, the bounds. Even at war, even when it costs him, there are lines he won't cross to win: not against what is sacred, not against his word. The battlefield is left at night, quiet, strewn with the fallen. Somewhere among them, a few are still awake.

648.title: Is Hanuman alive?
648.hook: two torches crossing a battlefield at night, and an old bear's surprising question
648.carry: sankat mochan: in trouble, hindus call on hanuman
648.howItsDone: Devotees call Hanuman Sankat Mochan, the remover of troubles, and turn to him in emergencies; Jambavan's question, is Hanuman alive, is often retold as a sign of his place in the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama and Lakshmana chose to endure Brahma's weapon, and fell with much of the army. Your line: maryada, lines Rama won't cross, even to win.
screen: `MARYADA: LINES RAMA WON'T CROSS, EVEN TO WIN.`

segments.voice: Two people are still on their feet: Vibhishana, who knows the weapons of Lanka, and Hanuman. It's night. They take torches and walk out across the battlefield, stepping between fallen warriors, looking for anyone still alive. Rama and Lakshmana lie in the arrows. Leader after leader lies still. Then, in the torchlight, they find Jambavan, the old king of the bears, so pierced with arrows he can't open his eyes, still breathing.
screen: `TWO STILL STANDING.` → `TORCHES ACROSS THE FIELD.` → `JAMBAVAN, STILL BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Vibhishana kneels and asks if he's alive. Jambavan knows the voice, though he can't see. And his first question isn't about Rama, or Lakshmana, or Sugriva his king. It's this: is Hanuman alive? Vibhishana is puzzled. Why Hanuman, and not the princes? Jambavan's answer is short and startling. If Hanuman lives, the whole army lives, even if it has been killed. If Hanuman is dead, we're dead, though we're still breathing. Hanuman steps forward and bows at the old bear's feet. Jambavan gives his orders. Go north, over the ocean, to the Himalaya. Between Mount Rishabha and Mount Kailasa is a mountain covered with healing herbs. He names four: one that brings back life, one that draws out arrows, one that restores the body's color, one that joins what's broken. Bring them, and the army will rise. Why ask about Hanuman first? Because Jambavan knows who can still save them. That same trust lives in one of Hanuman's best-loved names: Sankat Mochan, the remover of troubles. When trouble comes, at a hospital door, before a surgery, on a frightening night, many Hindus say Hanuman's name first, and the Hanuman Chalisa sings that he frees from trouble whoever holds him in mind, word and deed. Many also believe Hanuman is a chiranjivi, one who lives on, still near wherever Rama's name is sung. So the old bear's question has an answer devotees give gladly: yes.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you know who's in trouble right now. If you pray, say Hanuman's name slowly with the breath, or the familiar Jai Hanuman, holding that person before him. If you don't, ask Jambavan's question for them instead: who, and what, can still help? Let the breath steady you while you wait for the answer.

649.title: The herbs that hid
649.hook: a night flight the length of India, and herbs that hide
649.carry: the healing plants are alive, and holy
649.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a tulsi plant, watered daily and honored with a lamp; images of Hanuman flying with a mountain on his hand are found in temples, homes and calendars across India.

segments.voice: Yesterday: on a dark field, Jambavan asked first whether Hanuman was alive, and sent him north for four healing herbs. Your line: sankat mochan, in trouble, Hindus call on Hanuman.
screen: `SANKAT MOCHAN: IN TROUBLE, CALL ON HANUMAN.`

segments.voice: Hanuman climbs a mountain at the edge of the sea to push off, and he grows, the way he grew before the first leap. He presses down with his feet, and the mountain buckles under him. Then he's in the air, heading north. This isn't the hop to Lanka. This is the whole length of India, there and back, before dawn, with the army lying in the dark behind him.

Valmiki lets us ride along. Below him slide the ocean, then forests, rivers and towns, the hermitages of sages, the land unrolling under a flying monkey at night. Then the Himalaya rise ahead, snow and gold and rock. He sees Kailasa, the home of Shiva. He sees Mount Rishabha. And between them, just as Jambavan said, the mountain of herbs, glowing with its plants. Then the twist. Hanuman searches the slopes, and he can't find the four herbs. Valmiki says the plants knew someone had come for them, and hid; they made themselves invisible. The clock is running. Hanuman gets angry and speaks to the mountain: you won't help Rama? Then see what happens. He grips the whole peak, with its trees, its animals, its glowing herbs, tears it loose, and flies south with it, shining like a second sun. If you've grown up seeing Hanuman's picture, this is the one. But look at the detail Valmiki slips in: the herbs knew. In this story, plants aren't just things. They sense, they hide, they heal. That's an old Hindu thread. The Rig Veda has a whole hymn to the healing plants, calling them mothers and goddesses. And in many Hindu homes today, a tulsi plant, holy basil, grows in a pot by the door, watered each morning, a lamp lit beside it in the evening, honored as a goddess dear to Vishnu. When Hanuman spoke to that mountain, he was speaking to something alive.
screen: `THE LENGTH OF INDIA AT NIGHT.` · `THE HERBS HIDE.` · `HE LIFTS THE WHOLE PEAK.` · `THE HERBS KNEW.` · then, large: `THE HEALING PLANTS ARE ALIVE, AND HOLY.`

segments.voice: Find a plant near you, or picture one. Many Hindu families offer water to their tulsi each morning. segments.voice: Yesterday: the healing plants are alive, and holy. The plants hid, so Hanuman lifted the whole peak and flew it south like a second sun.

The monkeys still conscious see it first: a light in the northern sky, coming fast. Then they hear Hanuman's roar, and they roar back, weak and astonished. He sets down over the battlefield with a mountain in his hands, trees and rocks and all, glowing in the dark. And before anyone has picked a single leaf, something happens that nobody planned. The wind carries the scent of the herbs out over the field.
screen: `A LIGHT IN THE NORTH.` → `HANUMAN'S ROAR.` → `THE SCENT ON THE WIND.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, that's all it takes. The smell of the herbs drifts over the fallen, and they rise. Rama and Lakshmana breathe in, the arrows come out of them, and their wounds close. All around them the monkeys and bears get up, shaking themselves as if they'd been asleep. Valmiki notes something about the other side, too. The rakshasas who had died didn't rise, because Ravana had ordered his dead thrown into the sea, so the enemy wouldn't see how many he'd lost. Then Hanuman does something the famous picture doesn't show. He picks up the mountain again, flies it all the way back north, sets it in its place in the Himalaya, and returns to the camp. He doesn't keep the prize or put it on display. The work is done, so the mountain goes home. Many teachers see in this the Bhagavad Gita's teaching of nishkama karma, action without craving its fruit: your right is to the work alone, never to its rewards. Devotees hold up Hanuman as the one who lives it. In the epic's last book, when Rama offers him a gift, Hanuman asks only that his love for Rama never fade, and that he live as long as Rama's story is told. In a later telling, the Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas, Bharata shoots Hanuman down over Ayodhya as he passes. In Valmiki the trip is uninterrupted: north, south, north again, and back before the battle starts.

segments.voice: On a roadside shrine in North India, on the wall of a truck stop, in a grandmother's prayer room, the same picture keeps turning up: Hanuman in flight, mace in one hand, a mountain balanced on the other. Ask someone what's happening in it, and they'll probably tell a slightly different story from the one you've just heard. Lakshmana is dying. There's a physician. There's a deadline at dawn. That version is real too, and here's where it comes from.
screen: `A PICTURE ON SHRINE WALLS.` → `LAKSHMANA IS DYING.` → `A DEADLINE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Valmiki actually tells a herb flight twice. The first is the one you've followed: after Indrajit's Brahma weapon, the whole army down, Jambavan sending Hanuman north. The second comes near the very end of the war, when Lakshmana alone is struck by a spear, and Sushena, the monkey physician, sends Hanuman for the herbs again. Over time, in popular memory, the two have flowed together into one: Lakshmana wounded, the physician, the flight, the mountain, the race against the dawn. Later poets shaped that memory too. The Hanuman Chalisa, a hymn to Hanuman that devotees recite, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, says it in one line: he brought the life-giving herb, and Lakshmana lived, and Rama embraced him with joy. For some people that line is the whole story, even if they've never opened Valmiki. So which is right? Both belong to the tradition. Hindus have never had just one Ramayana. There's Valmiki's Sanskrit, Kamban's Tamil, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, and many more, told, sung and acted across India and beyond. Each keeps the heart; here, Hanuman as the one who brings healing, against the clock, when everyone else is helpless. And the story lives less on a shelf than in the reciting, which is one reason people say the Chalisa when someone they love is in hospital. Many tellings, one Rama.
